issue.title: ast_edit AX: AST validation does not block broken writes, and the schema contradicts the tool's two-step contract
issue.body:
### What happened?

Continuation of the editor-tool AX evaluation that produced #3033. Same method: drive the tool from its description alone, record every failure and hesitation, then read the source to root-cause. Fixtures in `tmp/editortest/`.

`ast_edit` has the most severe problems of the editing tools. The headline feature does not do what its name implies, the agent-facing schema contradicts the tool's actual contract, and a single one-line edit costs two calls plus a very large context dump.

### What did you expect to happen?

That "AST syntax validation" prevents me from writing a syntactically broken file, and that the schema describes how to actually drive the tool.

---

## 1. The schema lies about `force`, and it costs every caller a wasted call

Agent-facing schema (`packages/tools/src/tools/ast-edit.ts:142`):

    force: { description: 'Internal execution control. Managed automatically.' }

Internal contract (`packages/tools/src/tools/ast-edit/types.ts:164`):

> IMPORTANT: This tool ALWAYS operates in two steps:
> 1. First call: Preview changes (force: false or omitted)
> 2. Second call: Apply changes (force: true)

These directly contradict each other, and the one the agent reads is the wrong one. Nothing is "managed automatically" — `ast-edit-invocation.ts:195` returns a preview unless the caller passes `force: true`, and the response ends with `NEXT STEP: Call again with force: true to apply changes`.

Consequence: a first-contact caller believes the edit was applied when it was not. Once the caller learns the truth, the rational strategy is to always pass `force: true`, which skips the preview entirely and defeats the feature's purpose. Either way the design goal is lost.

Fix: describe the two-step contract in the agent-facing schema, or drop the preview phase.

## 2. AST validation does not block the write — it only narrates the damage

This is the important one. Applying an edit that provably breaks syntax:

    old_string: "  ship(id: string): Order {"
    new_string: "  ship(id: string): Order {{{"

Response:

    Successfully applied edit to: .../src/service.ts
    - Changes: 1 replacement(s) applied
    - AST validation: FAILED (new error introduced by this edit at line 1)

The broken file is on disk. `tsc` confirms: `error TS1005: ',' expected`, and four more.

So the tool detected the breakage, correctly attributed it to this edit ("new error introduced by this edit"), and wrote it anyway — under a message that opens with "Successfully applied edit". In the source, the validation result is only interpolated into the success string (`ast-edit-invocation.ts:481`); there is no gate.

A model skimming the first line reads "Successfully applied" and moves on. The tool is named `ast_edit` and sold on "AST syntax validation"; a validation that cannot refuse is a log line, not a validation.

Fix: when validation reports a *new* error introduced by this edit, refuse the write and return the error, with an explicit override if one is genuinely wanted. The tool already distinguishes new from pre-existing errors, so the hard part is done.

## 3. Syntax error locations are always reported as line 1

Every validation message points at line 1 regardless of where the damage is:

    - AST validation: FAILED (new error introduced by this edit at line 1)
    - AST errors: Syntax error at line 1, column 1

The actual break was near line 20; `tsc` reported line 29. Line 1 appears to be a placeholder, which makes the diagnostic useless for locating the problem.

## 4. Contradictory validation messaging

Reverting the broken edit produced, in one response:

    - AST validation: PASSED (edit may have resolved pre-existing error at line 1)
    - Pre-existing syntax errors: Yes at line 1 (not introduced by this edit)

PASSED and "Pre-existing syntax errors: Yes" in the same breath, both pointing at line 1, with a hedge ("may have"). The tool had enough information to know the file now parses cleanly.

## 5. "AST validation: PASSED" is reported for files that have no AST

Editing `notes.md` returns `- AST validation: PASSED`. There is no TypeScript AST for Markdown; nothing was validated. Reporting PASSED where validation was skipped is a false assurance. It should say "skipped (unsupported file type)".

## 6. The preview dumps the entire working set for a one-line edit

The preview for renaming one method emitted roughly 400 lines: every function, variable and import of ~25 unrelated files touched earlier in the session (`secure-store.ts`, `sandbox-containers.ts`, `jspSchema.ts`, broker tests, and so on), under `WORKING SET CONTEXT`. None of it was related to the edited file. Because the preview is mandatory (item 1), this cost is paid on every first call.

The genuinely useful part was the last few lines — `ENHANCED CONTEXT ANALYSIS` listing the four functions and one class in the file actually being edited, with correct line numbers. That part is good. The working-set dump should be dropped or made opt-in.

## 7. The symbol extractor emits garbage for prose files

Inside that dump, entries extracted from Markdown and YAML:

    project-plans/issue1985/plan.md:
      - class: ification()
      - class: ifies(key)
      - function: erred
      - function: ault
    docs/sandbox.md:
      - function: aults
      - function: ault(ADC)
    .github/workflows/nightly.yml:
      - function: aults

These are fragments of the words "classification", "specifies", "deferred", "default", "defaults" — the extractor is running a code-symbol regex over prose and reporting the tails of ordinary English words as declarations. Even if the dump is kept, non-code files should not be scanned this way.

## 8. File creation reports "0 replacement(s) applied"

Creating a file with an empty `old_string` succeeds and writes correct content, but reports:

    Successfully applied edit to: .../src/created.ts
    - Changes: 0 replacement(s) applied

"0 replacements" reads as a no-op. It should report that a file was created.

## 9. The `last_modified` mismatch error is double-encoded JSON

    {"error":"{\"message\":\"File ... mismatch. Expected mtime <= 1000000000000, but found 1785883468857.\",\"current_mtime\":1785883468857,\"your_mtime\":1000000000000}"}

An object has been `JSON.stringify`'d into the string error field. It also states the problem without the remedy (re-read the file, retry with the new timestamp).

---

## What works well

- The ambiguity error is the best of any editing tool here: `old_string appears 3 times in <file>. Provide more surrounding context to disambiguate.` — count plus remedy. Note `replace` reports the count but omits the remedy; `ast_edit`'s wording is the better model.
- `old_string` not found is clear and states no edits were made.
- The apply-phase success message is concise and appropriate.
- The `last_modified` concurrency check works correctly (only its formatting is poor).
- `ENHANCED CONTEXT ANALYSIS` for the edited file is accurate and genuinely useful.

## Suggested fixes, in priority order

1. Refuse the write when validation reports a new syntax error introduced by the edit. (item 2)
2. Fix the agent-facing `force` description to state the two-step contract. (item 1)
3. Report real error locations instead of line 1. (item 3)
4. Drop or gate the `WORKING SET CONTEXT` dump; keep the per-file analysis. (item 6)
5. Report "skipped" rather than "PASSED" for non-AST files, and stop extracting symbols from prose. (items 5, 7)
6. Report creation instead of "0 replacement(s)". (item 8)
7. Emit the `last_modified` error as a plain string with a remedy. (item 9)
8. Resolve the PASSED/pre-existing-errors contradiction. (item 4)

### Client information

0.11.0-nightly, branch at 75a5cb5d95

### Anything else we need to know?

Related: #3033 (apply_patch AX). Sibling evaluation of `replace` found it in good shape; the range editors have separate defects filed alongside this.

steps: Use ast_edit on src/service.ts with old_string `  ship(id: string): Order {` and new_string `  ship(id: string): Order {{{` and force: true, then check the file with tsc.
expected: ast_edit refuses to write an edit that its AST validation shows introduces a syntax error, leaving src/service.ts unchanged.
defect: ast_edit writes the broken code and reports "Successfully applied edit to: .../src/service.ts" together with "AST validation: FAILED"; tsc then reports `error TS1005: ',' expected`.

fault location.explanation: Only editData.error blocks the write; a failed editData.astValidation is ignored and the edit proceeds to writeEditResult; PR #3058 makes validation authoritative and rejects edits that introduce new syntax errors.
Writes the new content and builds a message that starts with 'Successfully applied edit' even when AST validation is FAILED; PR #3058 no longer writes in that case.
The agent-facing schema describes force as 'Internal execution control. Managed automatically.', contradicting the two-step preview/apply contract; PR #3058 rewrites the description.

Root cause: FIXED UPSTREAM IN https://github.com/vybestack/llxprt-code/pull/3058. In v0.10.0, ast_edit computes an AST validation of the edited content in calculateEdit, but executeApply only returns early on editData.error; the validation result is merely printed. writeEditResult therefore writes a syntactically broken file to disk and reports 'Successfully applied edit ... AST validation: FAILED'. In addition the schema tells the model that force is 'Internal execution control. Managed automatically.', so callers either believe a preview was applied or always pass force: true and skip the preview. Commit 0efa7c6 (PR #3058, 'make ast_edit validation authoritative') blocks writes whose validation shows newly introduced errors (new validation-categorizer logic, changes in edit-calculator.ts and ast-edit-invocation.ts) and describes the two-step contract in the force parameter. The fix first ships in v0.11.0, the pinned version, so the case is tested at v0.10.0.
